content.passage:
## The school games

Bill, Tom and Simon were best in four events in their school games. They were best in two jumping events: the high jump and the long jump. They were best in two races: the 100 metres and the 200 metres.

| Event | Bill | Tom | Simon |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| High jump | 1m 35 | 1m 45 | 1m 40 |
| Long jump | 3m 90 | 3m 50 | 3m 60 |
| 100 metres | 14 secs | 13 secs | 15 secs |
| 200 metres | 29 secs | 28 secs | 26 secs |

**Points**
First place - 3 points
Second place - 2 points
Third place - 1 point

questions.question: Who won the high jump?
Who jumped the farthest in the long jump?
Who ran the fastest in the 100 metres?
Who won the 200 metres race?

activities.title: Comparing the Athletes
activities.instruction: Complete the sentences using the correct comparative or superlative adverb based on the table from 'The School Games'.

content.feedback: Great effort! You've successfully completed the sentences. Keep it up! 🚀

sentences.text: In the high jump, Tom jumped the ___.

blanks.hint: Look at the high jump results for all three boys.

sentences.explanation: Tom's jump of 1m 45 was higher than Simon's (1m 40) and Bill's (1m 35), so he jumped the highest.

sentences.text: Bill jumped ___ than Simon in the long jump.

blanks.hint: Compare Bill's and Simon's long jump distances.

sentences.explanation: Bill jumped 3m 90 and Simon jumped 3m 60. Bill's jump was a greater distance, so he jumped farther.

sentences.text: In the 200 metres, Simon ran the ___.

blanks.hint: The shortest time means the fastest speed.

sentences.explanation: Simon's time of 26 seconds is the shortest, meaning he was the fastest of the three.

sentences.text: Tom ran ___ than Bill in the 100 metres.

blanks.hint: Compare Tom's and Bill's times for the 100 metres.

sentences.explanation: Tom's time was 13 seconds and Bill's was 14 seconds. A shorter time means a faster speed.

activities.instruction: Read the questions about the points and Challenge yourself! 📝 Select the best option for the correct answer.
activities.compensates: Calculation and discussion activity (TG 8.3, 3).

options.feedback: Tom had the fewest points. Try again.
Simon did well, but one boy had more points.

questions.question: Who had the most points at the end of the games?
questions.explanation: Points Calculation: Bill (2+3+2+2=9), Tom (3+1+3+2=9 - Error in TG, let's recalculate: Tom: 3+1+3+2=9. Simon: 2+2+1+3=8. Bill: 1+3+2+1=7. Okay, the TG has Bill=9, Simon=8, Tom=7. Let's use the TG's answer. Bill: HJ(1)=1, LJ(1)=3, 100m(2)=2, 200m(3)=1. Total=7. Tom: HJ(1)=3, LJ(3)=1, 100m(1)=3, 200m(2)=2. Total=9. Simon: HJ(2)=2, LJ(2)=2, 100m(3)=1, 200m(1)=3. Total=8. So Tom had the most points. Let's correct the question based on my calculation.

options.feedback: That's right! Simon had 8 points and Bill had 7.
Check the points again. Bill had 7 and Simon had 8.

options.text: They had the same number of points.
options.feedback: Their scores were close, but not the same.

questions.question: Who had more points - Simon or Bill?
questions.explanation: Based on the results: Simon scored 8 points (2+2+1+3) and Bill scored 7 points (1+3+2+1). Therefore, Simon had more points than Bill.

options.feedback: This is the base adjective. We need a superlative.
'Better' is used to compare two people.
Correct! 'Best' is used to compare three or more people.

questions.question: Overall, Tom did the ___ of the three boys.
questions.explanation: Tom had 9 points, the highest score. When comparing three people, we use the superlative form 'the best'.

activities.title: Understanding Future Forms
activities.instruction: Read each sentence and Challenge yourself! 📝 Select the best option for the correct meaning or form of the future tense.
activities.compensates: Teacher-led grammar explanation and drills on the board (Teacher Guide, page 253, section 2).

options.feedback: Correct! We use the present continuous (I'm playing) for fixed plans and arrangements.

options.text: I'm going to play football next week.
options.feedback: This describes a plan or intention, but the final arrangements might not be made yet.

options.text: I will play football next week.
options.feedback: This is a general statement about the future, often a spontaneous decision.

questions.question: Which sentence describes a fixed arrangement?
questions.explanation: The present continuous ('I am playing') is used for future events that are already arranged and confirmed.

options.feedback: Excellent! We use 'going to' for predictions based on present evidence (the dark clouds).
While possible, 'going to' is better here because we have evidence (the clouds).
This means it is raining right now, not in the future.

questions.question: Look at the dark clouds in the sky. It ______ soon.
questions.explanation: Use 'be going to' + verb to talk about something you expect to happen based on what you can see or know.

options.feedback: An arrangement is more fixed, like an appointment. This is more of a personal goal.
Correct! 'Going to' is often used to talk about future plans and intentions.
We usually use 'will' for spontaneous decisions made at the moment of speaking.

questions.question: The sentence 'I'm going to buy a motorbike when I am older' expresses a(n)...
questions.explanation: 'Be going to' is used to express a future plan or intention that has already been decided.

activities.title: Grammar: Which Happened First?
activities.instruction: Read each sentence. Challenge yourself! 📝 Select the best option for the action that happened first.
activities.compensates: Replaces teacher-led grammar explanation using a timeline on the board (PB68, Activity 2).

options.feedback: The past perfect 'had started' shows this action happened before the simple past 'got here'.
Correct! The past perfect 'had started' shows this action happened before the simple past 'got here'.

questions.question: In the sentence 'When I got here, the race had started', what happened first?
questions.explanation: We use the Past Perfect (had + past participle) to talk about an action that happened before another action in the past.

options.feedback: That's right! The past perfect 'had sold' tells us this happened first.

options.text: Bill went into the changing rooms.
options.feedback: The simple past 'went' shows this action happened after the first action.

questions.question: In the sentence 'Tom had sold the shoes to Simon before Bill went into the changing rooms', what happened first?
questions.explanation: The Past Perfect action always happens before the Simple Past action in the same sentence.

options.feedback: Correct! The bus leaving happened before Hassan arrived.
Hassan was too late. The bus had already gone.

questions.question: In the sentence 'The school bus had left when Hassan arrived', what happened first?
questions.explanation: The past perfect 'had left' indicates the first event in the past.

options.feedback: This action happened second. It is in the past simple.

questions.question: When I arrived at the shop, Ali had already closed it. Which action happened first?

questions.question: I couldn't buy anything to drink because Ahmed had sold everything. Which action happened first?

options.text: He came out of the supermarket.

Correct! The past perfect shows this action was completed before the next one began.

questions.question: After Rashid had finished his shopping, he came out of the supermarket. Which action happened first?

activities.title: Complete or Incomplete?
activities.instruction: Reading time! 📖 Read carefully and the group of words. Is it a complete sentence or just a part of a sentence (a clause)?
activities.compensates: Teacher-led board work identifying clauses and sentences.

options.feedback: This is a dependent clause. It needs more information to be a complete sentence. For example: 'If I had a compass, I would find my way home.'
Correct! This is a dependent clause that starts with 'If'. It needs a main clause to complete the thought.

questions.question: If I had a compass,
questions.explanation: Clauses starting with words like 'if', 'when', 'because', or 'so' often need another part to make a full sentence.

options.feedback: That's right! This is a complete thought with a subject (The forest) and a verb (is).
This is a main clause, which can stand alone as a complete sentence.

questions.question: The forest is full of dangerous animals.
questions.explanation: A main clause contains a subject and a verb and expresses a complete thought, so it can be a sentence by itself.

options.feedback: This clause tells us 'when' something happened, but not 'what' happened. It needs a main clause.

activities.title: Read the Story: Tom and Tariq - the medals
activities.instruction: Reading time! 📖 Read carefully and the story from Pupil's Book page 69. Then answer the questions below.
activities.compensates: Teacher-led reading of the story and asking comprehension questions (TG 8.8, Activities 3, 4, 6).

content.passage:
'If you see them, shout.' shouted Dick Bird.

'OK,' shouted Tariq. They both had to shout because there was a lot of noise. We were in Dick Bird's helicopter, flying over the mountains looking for the others. Somewhere down there Jim Cooper was lying on the ground with a broken leg.

'Follow that path, Dick,' Tariq shouted again.

'OK,' said Dick.

Five minutes later I saw them.

'Over: there!' This time I shouted. Chuck, Paul, Hans and David were waving arms and jackets like flags in the wind.

We landed.

'G'day, mate,' said Dick.

'G'day, mate,' said Jim.

'It means Hello,' I told Tariq.

Chuck and Hans tried to pick Jim up.

'No, no,' said Dick.' You mustn't move him. Not like that. You never know. It might be serious. We'll make a stretcher.'

Very carefully Tariq and I lifted Jim on to our stretcher, made from two pieces of wood and three sweaters, and carried him to the helicopter. Then we got in.

'I've been on the radio to Southport Hospital ,' said Dick.' They know we're coming.'

'What about the bus?' asked Tariq.

'Somebody from the town will drive it back,' said Dick. Then the helicopter started and we couldn't hear anything.

We left Jim at the hospital and a friend of Dick's drove us back to the camp.

'Tom! Tariq!' somebody shouted. It was Rod Border. He was running towards us.

'What have we done now?' I asked Tariq.

'Well done,' said Rod. 'You were fantastic. You're going to get a medal. Both of you. The WYC special medal.'

The next day everybody cheered as Rod Border pinned on Tariq's medal.'

'Thank you, Rod,' said Tariq, smiling. Then Rod pinned on my medal. He pressed too hard.

'Ouch!' I screamed. 'Ants! Ants!' I shouted as I jumped into the pool. 'Tom,' said Tariq, laughing. 'It was only this.' He was holding up the pin of the medal.

'Oh no,' I said. 'Why me? Why do these things always happen to me?'
